title: Finance U4·W4 — Gross Profit Fade, Estimate-to-Complete and the Cumulative Catch-Up
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the estimate is the entire company

Week 2 established that only one number in the WIP schedule is a judgment: the estimated cost at completion. Change the EAC and every downstream figure moves — percent complete, earned revenue, gross profit, over/under billing, the covenant ratio, the bonding capacity. Nothing else in a contractor’s financial statements has that reach. This is why gross profit fade — the tendency of a job’s estimated margin to deteriorate as it progresses — is the single most-watched metric in construction finance, and why the estimate-to-complete process is a CFO-level control rather than a project-management chore.

Fade, measured

Harbor Row Townhomes Phase 2, contract price $4,250,000 throughout:

HR-2 — estimated margin by quarter
Reporting dateEACEstimated gross profitEstimated margin
Q1 (original)$3,612,500$637,50015.00%
Q2$3,697,500$552,50013.00%
Q3$3,782,500$467,50011.00%
Final (actual)$3,825,000$425,00010.00%

Total fade = $637,500 − $425,000 = $212,500, or 5.00 points of margin, or 33.3% of the original estimated profit. That last framing is the one to say out loud to an owner: a third of the job’s profit disappeared, and it disappeared in increments small enough that no single quarter looked alarming.

Fade is a portfolio metric as much as a job metric. Track, every quarter, the change in estimated gross profit on all open contracts, and compute a fade rate: if a contractor consistently fades 3 to 5 points, its estimating system is biased, and every bid it submits — and every forecast the CFO builds on that backlog — is overstated by the same amount. Fade that is random is bad luck. Fade that is one-directional is a systematic defect, and the correction belongs in the estimating department, not the accounting department.

The cumulative catch-up, and how a profitable job posts a loss

Percent-of-completion accounting handles a change in estimate prospectively through a cumulative catch-up: the inception-to-date amounts are recomputed with the new estimate, and the entire difference lands in the current period. It is not a restatement of prior periods. It is a lump, and the lump can be brutal.

At Q2, cost to date on HR-2 was $2,588,250 and the EAC had been raised to $3,697,500.

  • Percent complete = $2,588,250 ÷ $3,697,500 = 70.00%
  • Earned revenue ITD = 70.00% × $4,250,000 = $2,975,000
  • Earned gross profit ITD = 70.00% × $552,500 = $386,750 (check: $2,975,000 − $2,588,250 = $386,750)
  • Prior (Q1) earned gross profit ITD was $414,375
  • Current-quarter gross profit = $386,750 − $414,375 = −$27,625

The job is still profitable — it will finish with $425,000 of gross profit — and yet it reported a gross loss of $27,625 in a quarter in which the crew built a quarter of a townhome complex. Decompose it and the mechanism is obvious:

  • Catch-up on prior progress: prior percent complete × change in estimated GP = 65.00% × (−$85,000) = −$55,250. The 65% already earned had been earned at 15% and is now restated to 13%.
  • Current-period progress at the new margin: change in percent complete × new estimated GP = 5.00% × $552,500 = +$27,625.
  • Sum: −$55,250 + $27,625 = −$27,625.

This decomposition is the CFO’s explanation to a lender, and it is worth memorizing: the quarter’s work was profitable; the quarter’s loss is a restatement of two prior quarters’ margin, recognized all at once because that is what the standard requires. It also explains why late EAC increases hurt disproportionately — the further along the job, the more prior progress there is to restate.

Building the estimate to complete properly

ETC = EAC − cost incurred to date, which at Q2 is $3,697,500 − $2,588,250 = $1,109,250. But that is the arithmetic definition, not the estimate. A defensible ETC is built bottom-up, by cost code, and then the EAC is derived from it — never the other way around:

HR-2 — bottom-up estimate to complete at Q2
ComponentAmountBasis
Remaining committed subcontracts$742,000Executed subcontract value less amounts billed
Remaining self-perform labor$214,250Remaining quantities × burdened crew rate
Remaining material and equipment$108,000Open POs plus unbought quantities at current pricing
Remaining contingency$45,000Unresolved risk items on the risk log
Estimate to complete$1,109,250

Four discipline points separate a real ETC from a wish. Unbought scope is the exposure — committed subcontracts carry price risk only for change orders, while unbought scope carries full market risk, so the ETC must show what fraction is bought out. Buyout savings are not profit until the scope is complete; the single most reliable predictor of fade is a project manager who recognizes early buyout savings and spends them on quality and schedule problems later. Contingency is drawn down deliberately, on a log, with a reason per draw. And the ETC must be reconciled to the schedule: a job forecast to finish in eight weeks that carries sixteen weeks of remaining labor hours has one of the two documents wrong.

The pathology to hunt is the stale EAC — a job where the EAC has never moved off the original budget. It is not evidence of good estimating; it is evidence that nobody is estimating. The classic pattern is an EAC frozen at budget until the job is 90%-plus complete, at which point the accumulated overrun arrives in one catastrophic quarter. A simple control catches it: flag every open job whose EAC is unchanged for two consecutive quarters and require a written re-forecast.

The loss job — recognized in full, immediately

Percent-of-completion spreads profit over the life of a contract. It does not spread losses. When the estimated cost at completion exceeds the contract price, the entire anticipated loss is recognized in the period it becomes known.

Northstar Services holds subcontract NS-19: contract price $640,000, revised EAC $715,000, so the forecast loss is $75,000. Cost to date is $429,000.

  • Percent complete = $429,000 ÷ $715,000 = 60.00%
  • Earned revenue = 60.00% × $640,000 = $384,000
  • Gross profit already recognized = $384,000 − $429,000 = −$45,000 (= 60.00% × −$75,000)
  • Additional provision required now = $75,000 − $45,000 = $30,000

Entry: DR Cost of revenue — provision for loss on contract $30,000 / CR Accrued contract loss $30,000. The accrual is a liability, released as the remaining loss is actually incurred, so no further loss hits the income statement on this job. The asymmetry is deliberate and it is a conservatism principle: profit is earned as performed, loss is a liability the moment it is probable and estimable. Practically, it means a CFO cannot defer a bad job into next year, and a job that flips to a loss position must be reported the same month it is identified.

The four causes of fade, priced

Post-mortem on the $212,500 of fade on HR-2:

HR-2 — fade attribution
CauseAmountOwner of the fix
Change-order work performed without an executed change order$62,000Contract administration
Framing labor overrun (hours, not rate)$48,500Estimating and field productivity
Material escalation on unbought scope$34,000Procurement timing
Extended general conditions from a six-week schedule slip$68,000Scheduling and owner claims
Total fade$212,500

The first line is the one a CFO must stop, because it is pure self-inflicted margin destruction: cost with no matching revenue, recognized the instant it is incurred. Meridian’s rule — no field work on an unexecuted change order without written CFO approval — exists because $62,000 of unauthorized work erased 1.5 points of margin on a job the field thought was going well.

Governing the estimate: who owns the EAC

Because the EAC drives the financial statements, it cannot be a number a project manager types into a field. It needs the same governance as any other significant accounting estimate, and the mechanism is a monthly job review with four fixed rules.

The estimate is proposed by the field and approved in accounting. The project manager owns the operational forecast — remaining quantities, crew productivity, schedule — because that is knowledge accounting does not have. The controller owns whether the resulting number is supported, consistent with the cost ledger, and reconciled to commitments. Neither party should be able to move reported gross profit alone; that is a segregation-of-duties principle applied to an estimate instead of a payment.

Every change is documented with a reason, in writing, at the cost-code level. “EAC increased $85,000” is not documentation. “Framing labor code 06-100 raised $48,500 for 620 additional crew hours at the burdened rate after the rework on buildings C and D” is documentation, and it is also the input to next year’s estimating correction.

Incentives are checked. If project managers are bonused on reported job margin, they are being paid to keep the EAC low, and fade becomes structural. Bonusing on final margin with a holdback, or on forecast accuracy rather than forecast level, removes the conflict. A CFO who complains about fade while paying for optimism is arguing with the incentive plan, and the incentive plan wins.

The forecast is validated after the fact. When a job closes, compare the final actual cost to the EAC at 50% complete and at 75% complete. That comparison, accumulated over twenty jobs, is the company’s estimating accuracy statistic — and it is the honest basis for the contingency the CFO carries in the company forecast and the risk premium built into the next bid. Everything else is opinion.

CMA bridge

The cumulative catch-up is Part 1-A (change in accounting estimate, recognized prospectively in the period of change) and the loss provision is Part 1-A loss-contingency accrual. The fade attribution table is Part 1-D variance analysis in construction dress — separating a quantity variance (labor hours) from a price variance (material escalation) from a scope variance (unapproved change orders). The ETC build and the contingency drawdown log are Part 1-B forecasting and Part 1-C performance management.

Practice and recap

  1. Measure fade as the change in estimated gross profit per job per quarter, and track it as a portfolio rate. One-directional fade is a systematic estimating defect.
  2. A change in EAC produces a cumulative catch-up = prior % complete × change in estimated GP, plus current progress at the new margin. HR-2 Q2: −$55,250 + $27,625 = −$27,625.
  3. Build the ETC bottom-up by cost code and derive the EAC from it. Flag any job whose EAC has not moved in two quarters.
  4. Recognize the FULL anticipated loss immediately: $75,000 forecast loss, $45,000 already in the numbers, accrue the remaining $30,000 now.
  5. Attribute fade to named causes with dollar amounts and an owner for each fix.

Recap: the EAC is the only judgment in the WIP schedule and it controls everything downstream; fade of $212,500 on HR-2 cost a third of the job’s profit in increments nobody flagged; raising the EAC forces a cumulative catch-up that made a profitable job report a $27,625 gross loss in one quarter; a defensible ETC is built bottom-up with unbought scope and contingency shown separately; and an anticipated loss is never spread — it is accrued in full the month it is known.

flashcards.back: The deterioration of a job's estimated margin as it progresses. HR-2: $637,500 (15.00%) → $425,000 (10.00%) = $212,500 fade, 5.00 margin points, 33.3% of the original estimated profit.

Track the change in estimated GP on all open contracts each quarter. Random fade is bad luck; one-directional fade is a systematic estimating bias that overstates every bid and every backlog-based forecast.

A change in EAC is a change in estimate, recognized PROSPECTIVELY: recompute inception-to-date amounts with the new estimate and put the entire difference in the current period. No prior-period restatement.
Current-period GP = (prior % complete × ΔEstimated GP) + (Δ% complete × new estimated GP). HR-2 Q2: 65.00% × (−$85,000) = −$55,250, plus 5.00% × $552,500 = +$27,625 → −$27,625.

flashcards.front: Why a profitable job posts a quarterly loss
flashcards.back: HR-2 will finish with $425,000 of GP but reported −$27,625 in Q2. The quarter's WORK was profitable; the quarter's LOSS is two prior quarters of margin restated at once. Late EAC increases hurt most — more prior progress to restate.

ETC = remaining committed subs $742,000 + remaining self-perform labor $214,250 + remaining material/equipment $108,000 + contingency $45,000 = $1,109,250. Derive the EAC from the ETC, never the reverse. EAC $3,697,500 − CTD $2,588,250 = $1,109,250.

An EAC frozen at the original budget is evidence nobody is estimating, not evidence of good estimating. The overrun arrives in one catastrophic quarter near completion. Control: flag every job whose EAC is unchanged two quarters running.

The FULL anticipated loss is recognized when known — losses are never spread. NS-19: contract $640,000, EAC $715,000 → $75,000 loss; CTD $429,000 = 60.00% complete, so −$45,000 is already booked. Accrue the remaining $30,000: DR provision for loss / CR accrued contract loss.

questions.q: HR-2's estimated gross profit fell from $637,500 (15.00%) to $425,000 (10.00%) on a $4,250,000 contract. Total fade is:
choices: $212,500, or 5.00 margin points and 33.3% of the original estimated profit

questions.q: At Q2 HR-2 has cost to date $2,588,250 and a revised EAC of $3,697,500. Earned gross profit inception-to-date is:
Prior inception-to-date earned gross profit was $414,375. Current-quarter gross profit is therefore:
choices: −$27,625 — a gross loss on a profitable job
questions.explain: $386,750 − $414,375 = −$27,625. The job still finishes profitable; the quarter absorbs the cumulative catch-up on prior progress.

questions.q: Decomposing that −$27,625, the catch-up on PRIOR progress is:
questions.explain: Prior percent complete × the change in estimated gross profit = 65.00% × (−$85,000) = −$55,250. Adding current progress at the new margin (5.00% × $552,500 = +$27,625) gives −$27,625.

questions.q: Subcontract NS-19 has a $640,000 contract price, a revised EAC of $715,000, and cost to date of $429,000. How much additional loss provision must be accrued now?
choices: $0 — losses are spread over the remaining life
questions.explain: The forecast loss is $75,000. At 60.00% complete ($429,000 ÷ $715,000), −$45,000 is already recognized. The full loss must be booked now, so accrue the remaining $30,000.

questions.q: Which item in an estimate to complete carries the MOST price risk?
choices: Unbought scope, which is exposed to full market pricing
questions.explain: Committed subcontracts fix price except for change orders; unbought scope is exposed to the market. A defensible ETC discloses what fraction of remaining cost is bought out.

questions.q: An open job's EAC has been unchanged at the original budget for three quarters. The best interpretation is:
choices: Nobody is re-estimating, and the accumulated overrun will land in one late quarter
The contract price must be wrong
questions.explain: A stale EAC is an absence of forecasting. The control is to flag any job whose EAC has not moved for two consecutive quarters and require a written re-forecast.
